items.title: L9: Two-way lookups and growth comparisons
items.source: Microsoft Support: INDEX, MATCH and MAX functions; Government Analysis Function guidance on presenting change
items.body:
A two-way lookup finds the value where a row and a column meet. The pattern is =INDEX(table, MATCH(row_label, row_labels, 0), MATCH(column_label, column_headers, 0)). The table range must be the data only, and the labels must be ranges of the same height and width as the table.

Use this table of cases closed. Row 1 holds the headings Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4 in B1:E1 and column A holds the regions in A2:A4.
North: 120, 150, 130, 160. South: 90, 110, 100, 140. East: 60, 80, 95, 85.
Then =INDEX(B2:E4,MATCH("South",A2:A4,0),MATCH("Q3",B1:E1,0)) returns 100. If a header is typed as "Q 3" with a space, MATCH returns #N/A. The row totals are North 560, South 440 and East 320, so the grand total is 1,320, and the quarter totals are Q1 270, Q2 340, Q3 325 and Q4 385.

To find the region with the highest figure in a quarter, combine MAX with MATCH: =INDEX(A2:A4,MATCH(MAX(E2:E4),E2:E4,0)) returns North for Q4, since 160 is the highest.

Be careful when you compare growth. From Q1 to Q4, South rose by 50 cases (90 to 140), North by 40 and East by 25. In percentage terms South rose 55.6 per cent, East 41.7 per cent and North 33.3 per cent. South has the largest rise by both measures here, but this will not always be so, since a small region can show a big percentage rise from a small base. State clearly which measure you are using, and give the base figures.

A share of the total is a part divided by the whole. North's share of Q4 closures is 160 divided by 385, which is 41.6 per cent. South's share of all closures over the year is 440 divided by 1,320, or 33.3 per cent.

Before you report any figure, check that totals add up and that the row and column labels were not changed.

questions.prompt: In the table, which formula returns East's figure for Q3?

options.text: =MATCH("East",A2:A4,0)+MATCH("Q3",B1:E1,0)
=INDEX(B2:E4,MATCH("East",A2:A4,0),MATCH("Q3",B1:E1,0))
=INDEX(A2:E4,MATCH("East",A2:A4,0),MATCH("Q3",B1:E1,0))
=INDEX(B2:E4,MATCH("Q3",A2:A4,0),MATCH("East",B1:E1,0))

questions.hint: The first MATCH locates the row and the second the column, and the INDEX range must start at B2 to line up with the headers.

questions.prompt: What value does the two-way lookup for East in Q3 return?
questions.hint: East's row is 60, 80, 95 and 85, and Q3 is the third column.

questions.prompt: A header was typed as 'Q 3' with a space and the lookup for 'Q3' fails. Which error appears?

options.text: #N/A
#REF!
#NAME?
#VALUE!

questions.hint: MATCH returns #N/A when it cannot find an exact match for the lookup text.

questions.prompt: What do the quarter totals Q1 to Q4 come to?
questions.hint: Add each column: for Q2 it is 150 + 110 + 80, which is 340.

questions.prompt: Which formula returns the region with the highest closure figure in Q4?

options.text: =MAX(INDEX(A2:A4,E2:E4))
=INDEX(E2:E4,MATCH(MAX(A2:A4),A2:A4,0))
=MATCH(MAX(E2:E4),A2:A4,0)
=INDEX(A2:A4,MATCH(MAX(E2:E4),E2:E4,0))

questions.hint: MAX finds the top value, MATCH finds its position, and INDEX turns the position into a region name.

questions.prompt: From Q1 to Q4, which region had the largest percentage rise?

options.text: South, with about 50%
North, with about 33.3%
South, with about 55.6%
East, with about 41.7%

questions.hint: South rose from 90 to 140, which is 50 divided by 90.

questions.prompt: A colleague says 'South rose by 50%'. What is wrong with that statement?

options.text: South's rise was 140%, because 140 is the final figure
The rise was 5.6%, since the quarters are 90 and 140
Nothing is wrong, as the percentage and the count are the same thing
50 is the rise in cases, whereas the percentage rise is about 55.6%

questions.hint: A count and a percentage are different measures, and the percentage divides the rise by the starting figure of 90.

questions.prompt: What is North's share of the total Q4 closures, to one decimal place?
questions.hint: 160 divided by the Q4 total of 385 gives 41.56%, which rounds to 41.6%.

questions.prompt: Why can a percentage rise mislead when comparing a small region with a large one?

options.text: Percentages cannot be calculated for small regions
Large regions always have lower percentage growth
The percentage is calculated on the end figure, which is always larger than the start
A small starting figure makes a small increase look large in percentage terms

questions.hint: Always show base figures alongside a percentage change so the reader can judge its size.

questions.prompt: South's quarter-by-quarter changes are +20, -10 and +40. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The biggest single movement was the rise of 20 in Q2, as it came right at the start
South fell in Q3, so the overall trend is downward
The changes show South rose by 40 over the year
The biggest single movement was the rise of 40 between Q3 and Q4

questions.hint: Over the year South rose by 50, and the largest step in one quarter was +40.

items.title: L9: Spreadsheets: FILTER, UNIQUE, SORT and dynamic arrays
items.source: Microsoft Support: dynamic array functions FILTER, UNIQUE, SORT; spilled array behaviour
items.body:
Dynamic array functions return several results that spill into the cells below and beside the formula. FILTER returns the rows that meet a condition: =FILTER(array, include, [if_empty]). UNIQUE returns the distinct values in a list. SORT sorts a range, and SORTBY sorts by another range. A spill range has to be clear of other data, otherwise the formula returns #SPILL!. You refer to a whole spill range with the hash sign, for example A2#.

Use this case list. Team: Alpha, Beta, Alpha, Gamma, Beta, Alpha, Gamma, Beta. Status: Open, Closed, Closed, Open, Open, Open, Closed, Open. Amount: 100, 250, 75, 300, 120, 90, 60, 210. The first row is Alpha, Open, 100, and the data sits in A2:C9.

=UNIQUE(A2:A9) returns three teams: Alpha, Beta and Gamma. =FILTER(C2:C9,B2:B9="Open") returns the five open amounts: 100, 300, 120, 90 and 210. =SUM(FILTER(C2:C9,B2:B9="Open")) returns 820. For the amount of open cases for Alpha only, use a double condition: =FILTER(C2:C9,(A2:A9="Alpha")*(B2:B9="Open")), where multiplying means AND. That returns 100 and 90, which total 190. Using plus instead of the multiplication sign means OR.

=SORT(C2:C9,1,-1) sorts the amounts from largest to smallest, so the first value is 300. =FILTER(A2:C9,B2:B9="Closed","None") returns the three closed rows, and if there were none it would display the text None instead of #CALC!.

Dynamic arrays need a recent version of Excel. If a colleague opens the file in an older version, the formula is shown as an old-style array formula or returns an error, so check compatibility before sharing.

Compare with COUNTIFS for a simple count: =COUNTIFS(A2:A9,"Beta",B2:B9,"Open") returns 2. COUNTIFS is easier to follow for counts, whereas FILTER suits a list of records that you want to read.

questions.prompt: In the case list, how many different teams does =UNIQUE(A2:A9) return?
questions.hint: The teams are Alpha, Beta and Gamma, although they appear several times each.

questions.prompt: What does =SUM(FILTER(C2:C9,B2:B9="Open")) return?
questions.hint: The open amounts are 100, 300, 120, 90 and 210.

questions.prompt: What is the total of open amounts belonging to Alpha only?
questions.hint: Alpha's open cases are 100 and 90.

questions.prompt: In a FILTER with two conditions, what does multiplying the tests with an asterisk do?

options.text: It applies OR, so either test can be true
It multiplies the amounts by each other
It applies AND, so both tests must be true
It sorts the results by the first test

questions.hint: True is 1 and false is 0, so the product is 1 only when both are true.

questions.prompt: What is the first value returned by =SORT(C2:C9,1,-1)?
questions.hint: The -1 means descending order, so the largest value is first.

questions.prompt: The fourth argument in =FILTER(A2:C9,B2:B9="Closed","None") is used for what purpose?

options.text: It formats the result as text
It shows the word None if no rows are found
It sets the number of rows returned
It filters out the closed rows from the result

questions.hint: The if_empty argument stops an error appearing when nothing matches.

questions.prompt: A FILTER formula returns #SPILL!. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The formula has no closing bracket
The workbook has been saved as a PDF
The source data contains too many numbers for the function to process in one go
There is data in cells where the results need to appear

questions.hint: A spill range must be clear of other content.

questions.prompt: What does =COUNTIFS(A2:A9,"Beta",B2:B9,"Open") return?
questions.hint: Beta has three rows and two of them are open: 120 and 210.

questions.prompt: Why might you prefer COUNTIFS to FILTER for a simple count?

options.text: FILTER cannot deal with text
It is simpler to read and works in older versions of Excel
COUNTIFS can spill results into other cells whereas FILTER can only return one value
COUNTIFS sorts the records automatically

questions.hint: Use the simplest tool that does the job and that colleagues can open.

questions.prompt: You send a workbook with dynamic array formulas to a colleague who has an old version of Excel. What is a likely outcome?

options.text: The formulas may show as old-style array formulas or return errors
Excel converts them to values for you
The colleague is unable to open the file
The formulas work in the same way as before because Excel converts them automatically

questions.hint: Dynamic array functions are not supported in older versions, so check before sharing.

items.title: L9: Reconciling figures and finding the source of a mismatch
items.source: Government Analysis Function: guidance on spreadsheets and quality assurance; Microsoft Support: pivot table troubleshooting
items.body:
A reconciliation proves that two sets of figures agree, or shows exactly why they do not. When a pivot table total differs from the source total, or one report disagrees with another, work through the usual causes in order, rather than guessing.

Start by checking scope. Do the two figures cover the same time period, the same population and the same definition? A report of cases received in March and a report of cases received between 1 March and 1 April will differ by a day's worth. Check whether one includes withdrawn cases and the other does not.

Next, check the data. Duplicate rows can inflate a total. Blank rows or rows missed because the pivot table's range did not include new records can reduce it. Numbers stored as text are ignored by SUM and are counted in COUNT only if they look numeric. Text with a trailing space can split a category into two. Filters left on can hide rows from a total: SUBTOTAL ignores filtered-out rows, whereas SUM does not.

Then check the method. A formula may refer to the wrong range, or one total may be rounded before it is added. Rounding can cause totals to be 99 or 101 per cent when shares are added, which is not an error: say that figures may not sum due to rounding.

Work in a systematic way. Start with the total difference, split it by category, and find the category where the gap sits. If the gap is 40 and exactly one category is 40 higher in one source, look at that category's records. Check whether the difference equals the value of a single row, which suggests a missing or duplicated record.

Keep a note of each check and the result. An audit trail lets another person repeat the work, and it protects you if the figure is challenged. Do not 'plug' a difference with an adjustment you cannot explain.

questions.prompt: A pivot table total is 40 lower than the source total, and one source row has the value 40. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The source total includes a duplicate of that row
That row was not included in the pivot table's range or was filtered out
Numbers in the pivot table have been converted to text, so they were left out of the total
The pivot table has been rounded

questions.hint: A gap equal to one row's value points to a missing or hidden record.

questions.prompt: The pivot total is 40 higher than the source total, and a row with 40 appears twice. What should you do?

options.text: Change the source total to match the pivot table and note the difference in the file
Subtract 40 from the pivot table total
Confirm that it is a true duplicate and then remove one copy
Remove both copies to be safe

questions.hint: Check the cause in the data and fix it there, rather than adjusting a total.

questions.prompt: Two reports show different case counts: one counts 1 March to 31 March and the other counts 1 March to 1 April. What is the first thing to check?

options.text: Whether they cover the same period
Whether both use the same font
Which team wrote each report
Whether one report has a better chart

questions.hint: A difference in scope explains many mismatches, so compare definitions first.

questions.prompt: Which function ignores rows that have been hidden by a filter?

options.text: SUBTOTAL
MAX
COUNTA
SUM

questions.hint: SUBTOTAL can exclude filtered-out rows, whereas SUM includes all of them.

questions.prompt: Shares of 33%, 33% and 33% add up to 99%. How should this be handled?

options.text: Remove the percentages from the table
Change one share to 34% without saying so, so that the table adds up to 100%
Add a note that figures may not sum to 100% because of rounding
Report only two of the three shares

questions.hint: Rounding differences are normal, and a footnote explains them.

questions.prompt: A total shows 1,200 in one report and 1,160 in another, and the gap is 40. What is the most systematic first step?

options.text: Ask the author of the higher figure to recheck it and use their answer as the correct one
Break the totals down by category and find where the 40 sits
Use the average of the two totals
Add 40 to the lower figure

questions.hint: Narrowing down by category localises the cause.

questions.prompt: Which is a sensible way to record a reconciliation?

options.text: Write only the final answer
Note each check and its result so someone else can repeat it
Keep the checks in your head
Delete the working once the figure agrees, since it is no longer needed by anyone

questions.hint: An audit trail allows others to verify and protects the analyst.

questions.prompt: Why is 'plugging' a difference with an unexplained adjustment poor practice?

options.text: It makes the sheet harder to print
It uses too many cells
It hides an error that could affect other figures and cannot be justified
It always causes a circular reference, which stops the workbook from calculating at all

questions.hint: Unexplained adjustments undermine confidence in all the numbers.

questions.prompt: Text with a trailing space, such as 'Housing ', appears in a column of categories. What effect might it have in a pivot table?

options.text: It deletes the row from the pivot table and removes its amount from the total
It sorts the category to the top
It can create a separate category from 'Housing'
It converts the column to numbers

questions.hint: Different strings are treated as different items.

questions.prompt: A colleague's total ignores some numbers stored as text. How could you detect this?

options.text: Check the colour of the cell borders and the alignment of each number in the column
Sort the column from Z to A
Look at the file size
Compare COUNT with COUNTA, or look for the green triangle and left alignment

questions.hint: COUNT ignores text and COUNTA counts it, so a difference suggests text-stored numbers.

items.title: L9: Assuring a spreadsheet: checks, reviews and the AQuA Book
items.source: HM Treasury: The Aqua Book: guidance on producing quality analysis for government; Government Analysis Function spreadsheet guidance
items.body:
Government analysis supports decisions with large consequences, so spreadsheets that feed them need assurance. The AQuA Book (HM Treasury) is guidance on producing quality analysis. It says analysis should be fit for purpose, proportionate to risk, and carried out by competent people. It describes verification, which checks that the analysis was built correctly, and validation, which checks that it is the right analysis and meets the need. Where the stakes are high, independent review adds confidence.

Good practice for a spreadsheet model includes the following. Separate inputs, calculations and outputs, so a reader can see what drives the result. Put each assumption in one labelled cell, instead of hard-coding the number inside formulas. Use consistent formulas across a row or column; a single different formula in a series is a classic error and is often hard to spot, so use Go To Special to find inconsistencies. Keep a README or notes sheet with the purpose, sources, version, author and a record of changes.

Build checks into the model. A check cell can compare a total computed in two ways and show a flag when they differ. Test with simple numbers where you know the answer. Try extreme values to see if the model behaves sensibly. Use Trace Precedents and Trace Dependents to follow the flow of calculations.

Avoid circular references unless they are deliberate and documented. Avoid volatile functions in large models, because they recalculate constantly and slow the file. Protect formulas against accidental overwriting.

Review by a second person, sometimes called a four-eyes check, catches errors the builder cannot see. The reviewer should not just look at the answer but should test the logic. Record who reviewed it, when and what they covered.

Keep a version log and store the master in a controlled location. Famous failures show how a small spreadsheet error, such as a wrong range in a sum, can lead to a serious misstatement.

questions.prompt: In the AQuA Book, what does verification check?

options.text: That the analysis answers the right question
That the analysis was built correctly
That the results are popular with ministers
That the model uses the latest software

questions.hint: Verification checks the build, and validation checks that it is the right analysis for the need.

questions.prompt: What does validation check, in AQuA Book terms?

options.text: That the model is no longer than 20 sheets and takes less than a minute to open
That the file is stored securely
That every formula is typed correctly
That the analysis is the right one and fits the need

questions.hint: Validation tests whether the analysis is fit for its purpose.

questions.prompt: Why is it better to put an assumption such as an inflation rate in one labelled cell?

options.text: It makes the workbook look longer
It can be seen and changed in one place, rather than being buried in formulas
It stops Excel recalculating
It prevents anyone from reading the rate, which protects the department from challenge

questions.hint: Hard-coded numbers inside formulas are hard to find and audit.

questions.prompt: In a row of 12 monthly totals, one cell has a different formula from the others. What is the best way to find such inconsistencies?

options.text: Sort the row from smallest to largest
Use Go To Special to select cells with formulas that differ from their neighbours
Check the font colour of each cell
Count the characters in each cell

questions.hint: Inconsistent formulas are a common error and the tool highlights them.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a check cell in a model?

options.text: To store the model's assumptions
To hide errors from the user
To flag when two calculations of the same total disagree
To protect the sheet from editing by anyone other than the person who built it

questions.hint: Built-in checks catch errors as soon as inputs or formulas change.

questions.prompt: A second person reviews your model. Which review is most useful?

options.text: Testing the logic and the formulas, not only checking that the final answer looks right
Reading the summary sheet only
Checking that the layout matches the template
Checking that the model uses the department's colours

questions.hint: A reviewer should challenge how the answer is produced.

questions.prompt: Why should circular references normally be avoided?

options.text: They only work in older versions
They can make results unstable or wrong and are hard to audit
They are a security risk
They stop the file from being saved until the loop in the formulas is resolved

questions.hint: If a circular reference is deliberate it must be documented and tested.

questions.prompt: What should a notes or README sheet in a model contain?

options.text: A copy of the minister's briefing and the final sign-off from the director
Only the final result
The passwords for the sheet
The purpose, sources, version, author and record of changes

questions.hint: Documentation lets a new user understand and trust the model.

questions.prompt: What does 'proportionate to risk' mean for the level of assurance?

options.text: Assurance is optional for anything below ministerial level
Only analyses by junior staff need checks
Every spreadsheet needs the same number of checks
High-stakes or complex analysis needs more checking than a low-risk, simple calculation

questions.hint: Effort is matched to the impact of an error and the complexity of the work.

questions.prompt: Why test a model with simple numbers where you already know the answer?

options.text: To check that it gives the result you expect before relying on real data
To make the file smaller
To remove the need for a review, because testing proves that the model is correct
To make the formulas faster

questions.hint: Simple test cases reveal logical errors that real data may hide.

items.title: L9: Flow models: backlogs, receipts and clearance times
items.source: Government Analysis Function: guidance on forecasting and presenting uncertainty; HM Treasury Green Book on assumptions and sensitivity
items.body:
Many operational questions are flow problems: work arrives, work is cleared, and what is left is the backlog. The basic equation is: closing backlog = opening backlog + received - closed. In a spreadsheet, put the weeks down the rows, opening backlog in one column, receipts and closures in the next, and closing backlog as a formula that becomes the next week's opening.

Suppose a team starts with a backlog of 1,200 cases, receives 400 a week and closes 460 a week. Each week the backlog falls by 60, so after four weeks it is 1,200 - 4 x 60 = 960. The time to clear is the backlog divided by the net weekly reduction: 1,200 divided by 60 is 20 weeks.

The answer is very sensitive to the net rate. If closures rise to 480, the net reduction is 80 and the backlog clears in 15 weeks. If receipts rise to 420 and closures remain at 460, the net reduction is 40 and it takes 30 weeks. A small change in either flow changes the answer a lot, because the net difference is small compared with each flow. If closures fall to or below receipts, the backlog never clears and the formula breaks down, so test for this and show a message.

These are simple projections that assume constant rates. In reality, receipts vary by season and capacity changes. Present a range or scenarios rather than one number, state the assumptions, and say that it is an illustration and not a forecast. A sensitivity table that shows clearance time against different closure rates helps the reader see the risk.

Be clear about what is included. Does the backlog count only cases past their target date, or all open cases? A backlog of cases within target is normal working stock, not delay. Agree the definition before reporting.

Where the figure supports a decision on staffing, show how many extra closures per week are needed to meet a target date. To clear 1,200 cases in 10 weeks with 400 received weekly, closures must average 1,200 divided by 10 plus 400, which is 520 a week.

questions.prompt: A backlog of 1,200 grows by 400 received and falls by 460 closed each week. What is the backlog after four weeks?
questions.hint: The weekly net fall is 60, and four weeks reduces the backlog by 240.

questions.prompt: With the same figures, how many weeks does it take to clear the backlog?
questions.hint: 1,200 divided by the net weekly reduction of 60.

questions.prompt: Closures rise to 480 a week with receipts at 400. How long does it take to clear 1,200 cases?

options.text: 30 weeks
12 weeks
20 weeks
15 weeks

questions.hint: The net reduction becomes 80, and 1,200 divided by 80 is 15.

questions.prompt: Receipts rise to 420 a week while closures stay at 460. What happens to the time to clear 1,200 cases?

options.text: It falls to 15 weeks
It rises to 25 weeks
It rises to 30 weeks
It stays at 20 weeks

questions.hint: The net reduction falls to 40, so 1,200 divided by 40 is 30.

questions.prompt: Why is the clearance time so sensitive to small changes in receipts or closures?

options.text: Because the backlog is always rounded
Because closures are counted twice
The net difference between two large flows is small, so a small change alters it proportionally a lot
Because receipts are not measured weekly

questions.hint: A change of 20 in a net of 60 is a big proportional change.

questions.prompt: Closures fall to 400 a week while receipts remain at 400. What does the clearance time formula give?

options.text: The backlog clears in 4 weeks
The backlog never clears, so the formula divides by zero and must be handled
The backlog clears in 1 week
The backlog clears in 20 weeks, exactly as it did when closures were 460 a week

questions.hint: With no net reduction, the clearance time is infinite, so the model needs a test.

questions.prompt: How many closures per week are needed to clear 1,200 cases in 10 weeks if 400 arrive each week?
questions.hint: The backlog needs a reduction of 120 a week on top of matching the 400 received.

questions.prompt: Why should you present clearance times as scenarios or a range?

options.text: Because a range is easier to chart
Because spreadsheets cannot calculate a single answer
Rates change in practice, so a single figure suggests more certainty than exists
Because managers prefer longer reports

questions.hint: Honest presentation of uncertainty helps the reader judge the risk.

questions.prompt: Why should you agree a definition of 'backlog' before reporting it?

options.text: Because a backlog is always defined in law
Cases within target are normal work in progress, and counting them would overstate the delay
Because only closed cases count
Because the definition changes the formula in Excel

questions.hint: Different definitions can give very different numbers for the same team.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to describe a projection that assumes constant rates?

options.text: As a prediction of what will happen if the team keeps working as it does now
As an official target
As an illustration based on stated assumptions, not a forecast
As a guarantee of the end date

questions.hint: A projection shows consequences of assumptions, not certainty.

items.title: L9: Percentages that mislead: chains, compounding and rounding
items.source: Office for National Statistics: percentage change guidance; Government Analysis Function: communicating uncertainty and change
items.body:
Percentages are easy to mishandle, and an error in a senior briefing can undermine trust in the whole paper. Learn the common traps.

A percentage rise followed by the same percentage fall does not return to the start. Take a price of 200. Add 10 per cent and you have 220. Take off 10 per cent of 220, which is 22, and you have 198, not 200. The second percentage applies to a different base.

Percentages compound. Growth of 5 per cent a year for three years is not 15 per cent. It is 1.05 x 1.05 x 1.05 = 1.157625, an increase of about 15.8 per cent. For a figure of 400, the three-year result is about 463, not 460.

To remove a percentage that has been added, divide, don't subtract. If a price including 20 per cent VAT is 120, the price before VAT is 120 divided by 1.2, which is 100. Taking 20 per cent off 120 gives 96, which is wrong because the 20 per cent was calculated on the smaller original price.

A change in a rate is described in percentage points. A rate that rises from 8 per cent to 10 per cent has risen by 2 percentage points, which is a 25 per cent increase in the rate (2 divided by 8). Both statements are true, but they must not be confused. Use percentage points for differences between percentages.

Rounding can cause totals to disagree. If three equal categories each hold one third, rounding each to a whole percentage gives 33, 33 and 33, which add to 99. Say that figures may not add due to rounding, or show one decimal place. Do not adjust a figure silently.

Always give the base figures with the percentages. A fall of 50 per cent from 4 to 2 and from 4,000 to 2,000 are the same in percentage terms but very different in scale. Be explicit about the period and the base when you report a percentage change.

questions.prompt: A price of 200 rises by 10% and then falls by 10%. What is the final price?
questions.hint: The second percentage applies to 220, so 22 is taken off.

questions.prompt: Growth of 5% a year for three years is closest to what total increase?
questions.hint: 1.05 cubed is 1.157625, so the increase is about 15.8%.

questions.prompt: A figure of 400 grows by 5% a year for three years. What is the result, rounded to the nearest whole number?
questions.hint: 400 multiplied by 1.157625 is 463.05.

questions.prompt: A price including 20% VAT is £120. What is the price before VAT?
questions.hint: Divide by 1.2: the VAT was calculated on the original price.

questions.prompt: A colleague takes 20% off £120 to remove VAT and gets £96. What is their mistake?

options.text: They should have taken 25% off the original price, because 20% is a quarter of 80
They should have added 20%
They applied 20% to the VAT-inclusive price rather than dividing by 1.2
They used the wrong number of decimal places

questions.hint: The 20% was added to the net price, so it must be removed by division.

questions.prompt: A rate rises from 8% to 10%. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: It rose by 20 percentage points
It rose by 25 percentage points
It rose by 2%, which is also a 2% increase in the rate
It rose by 2 percentage points, a 25% increase in the rate

questions.hint: Percentage points describe the difference between two percentages, and 2 divided by 8 is 25%.

questions.prompt: Three equal categories are each shown as 33%. What should a table note say about the total of 99%?

options.text: That one category has been left out of the table and needs to be added back in
That the data contains an error
That figures may not sum to 100% because of rounding
That the total has been adjusted

questions.hint: Rounded shares of a whole often miss 100%, and the note avoids confusion.

questions.prompt: A report says 'complaints halved'. The count fell from 4 to 2. What should the briefing add?

options.text: Nothing, as the percentage speaks for itself
A claim that service quality has doubled
A prediction that the trend will continue
The actual numbers, as a halving from 4 to 2 is a small change in absolute terms

questions.hint: Base figures help the reader judge the importance of a percentage change.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct way to describe a move from 20% to 15%?

options.text: A fall of 5%
A fall of 25 percentage points
A fall of 5 percentage points
A fall of 0.25%

questions.hint: The difference between two percentages is in percentage points, and relative to the starting rate it is a 25% fall.

questions.prompt: A figure falls 50% in one year and then rises 50% the next. Compared with the start, the figure is:

options.text: 25% higher
50% lower
The same as at the start
25% lower

questions.hint: 1 x 0.5 x 1.5 = 0.75 of the original.

items.title: L9: Briefing a Director General on a data problem
items.source: Civil Service Code; Code of Practice for Statistics; Success Profiles: communicating and influencing, seeing the big picture
items.body:
When a data problem threatens a decision or a publication, the Director General (DG) needs a short note that tells them what happened, how serious it is and what to do. Do not wait until you have the complete answer. Senior readers prefer an early honest warning with a plan over a late surprise.

Lead with the answer in the first two sentences: what is wrong, how big the effect is and what you recommend. For example: 'The caseload figure published in May is overstated by about 4 per cent because of duplicate records. We recommend correcting it on Thursday and informing the minister's office today.' Follow with the key facts, your confidence in them, what is still unknown and when you will know more.

State the impact in terms the reader cares about: which published figures or decisions are affected, who has used them, and whether any customer has been harmed. Separate what you know from what you suspect. Give a range when you cannot give a single estimate, such as 'between 3 and 5 per cent', and say how you arrived at it.

Set out the options for dealing with it, such as correcting now, correcting with the next release, or investigating further first. For each, give the risk to trust and the practical effect. The Code of Practice for Statistics expects that errors are corrected quickly and transparently. Under the Civil Service Code, officials must not conceal a mistake or mislead.

Say what has already been done to stop the problem growing, such as stopping a feed of data or alerting users. Name an owner and a time for each action.

Be careful about tone. Avoid blame and avoid dramatic language. Facts and calm judgement build confidence. Check every number before sending, and keep the note within a page, with detail in an annex.

questions.prompt: Which opening is best for a note to a DG about a data error?

options.text: Following a number of conversations, a decision is needed on how to proceed on the data.
There may be some concerns about the quality of the data used in the May publication.
The May caseload figure is overstated by about 4% because of duplicate records, and we recommend correcting it on Thursday.
I am writing to update you on a data issue that has been under review by the team for some time.

questions.hint: A senior reader needs the problem, the size and the recommendation straight away.

questions.prompt: You do not yet know the exact size of an error. What is the best approach in the note?

options.text: Give the lowest estimate so it looks smaller
Wait until you can give a single exact figure
Give a range, say how you arrived at it and when you will know more
Leave the figure out and say it is under review until the exact value is known

questions.hint: A range with a basis is more useful than silence or false precision.

questions.prompt: Why should the note separate what you know from what you suspect?

options.text: So that the note looks longer
So the reader can judge how far to rely on each part
So that the team cannot be blamed
So the reader can ignore the suspected items and concentrate on the confirmed ones

questions.hint: Clear separation helps a senior reader weigh the risks.

questions.prompt: What does the Code of Practice for Statistics expect when an error is found in published statistics?

options.text: That it is corrected quietly at the next annual release
That only the minister is told
That it is corrected quickly and transparently
That it is left alone if the effect is small

questions.hint: Trustworthiness depends on openness about errors.

questions.prompt: Which option for handling a published error is most consistent with the Civil Service Code?

options.text: Tell the minister's office promptly and correct the figure openly
Wait for the next release to correct it
Change the figure on the website without comment, so that the error attracts less attention
Say nothing until a user raises the matter

questions.hint: Honesty and integrity mean not concealing mistakes.

questions.prompt: Which element should the note include for each action?

options.text: A summary of past errors
A list of those to blame
A page of technical detail
An owner and a time

questions.hint: Named owners and timings make the plan credible.

questions.prompt: How should the impact of the error be described?

options.text: In terms of which figures or decisions are affected, who used them and whether anyone was harmed
In terms of how embarrassing it might be
In terms of how many hours the team spent finding it
In terms of the software used

questions.hint: The reader cares about consequences.

questions.prompt: The DG asks 'How confident are you?' What is the best style of answer?

options.text: 'It is difficult to say at this point.'
'We are certain it is exactly 4%.'
'I would not like to speculate.'
'Quite confident in the direction, less sure of the size: I would put the error at 3 to 5% and will confirm by Wednesday.'

questions.hint: State confidence honestly and say how and when uncertainty will be reduced.

questions.prompt: What tone is most helpful in a note on a data error?

options.text: Factual and calm, avoiding blame and drama
Apologetic and emotional, to show how seriously the team takes it
Defensive and brief
Technical and detailed

questions.hint: Calm judgement builds confidence and supports good decisions.

questions.prompt: Where does the technical detail of the investigation belong?

options.text: In the first paragraph
In an annex that the DG can read if they wish
In a separate email sent later, once the DG has read the main note
In the subject line

questions.hint: The main note must stay short, with detail available for those who want it.

items.title: L9: Editing an executive summary for a senior reader
items.source: GOV.UK style guide; Civil Service Success Profiles: communicating and influencing; Plain English Campaign
items.body:
An executive summary is the part of a paper most likely to be read by a senior reader, so it must stand alone. It should answer four questions in order: what is the issue, what did we find, what do we recommend, and what do we need from the reader. It should be short, usually under a page, and written in plain English, with numbers that match the main text.

Consider this weak draft: 'The department has, over a period of time, been conducting a review of processes relating to claims handling, and it has been found that there are a number of areas in which improvements could potentially be made. It is felt that consideration should be given to a number of options, which are set out in the paper, in order that a way forward might be agreed.'

It has several problems. It is vague: 'a number of areas' and 'potentially' say nothing. It buries the finding. It does not recommend anything, and it hides who is doing what with passive phrases. It does not say what the reader should decide or by when.

A stronger version reads: 'Claims now take 31 days on average, against a target of 20. Most of the delay arises at the evidence-checking step, where 60 per cent of cases wait for a second review. We recommend removing the second review for low-risk claims. This would cut the average to about 22 days at a cost of £80,000 a year. Please agree by 14 March so we can start in April.'

Notice the techniques: figures with a comparison (31 days against 20), a clear location of the problem, a specific recommendation, cost and benefit, and a deadline with a reason. It uses short sentences and active verbs.

When you edit a summary, delete every sentence that does not help the reader decide. Check that the recommendation in the summary matches the one in the conclusion. Read it as someone who will only read this page.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of the opening line 'The department has, over a period of time, been conducting a review...'?

options.text: It uses the present tense
It is vague and delays the finding the reader needs
It mentions the department by name instead of saying what the department found
It is too short

questions.hint: A summary should start with the finding or issue, not the history of the review.

questions.prompt: Which phrase in the weak draft is most clearly vague?

options.text: 'a number of areas in which improvements could potentially be made'
'claims handling'
'the department'
'set out in the paper'

questions.hint: It gives no number, no area and no size of improvement.

questions.prompt: Which element makes the stronger version 'Claims now take 31 days on average, against a target of 20' effective?

options.text: It avoids numbers
It explains the history of the review
It gives a figure with a comparison
It uses the passive voice

questions.hint: A comparison shows how big the problem is.

questions.prompt: Why does the stronger version name the evidence-checking step?

options.text: It says where the problem sits, so the recommendation makes sense
It replaces the need for a recommendation, as the finding already speaks for itself
It makes the summary longer
It shows who is to blame

questions.hint: Locating the cause links the finding to the proposed action.

questions.prompt: What does the sentence 'Please agree by 14 March so we can start in April' provide?

options.text: A suggestion that the paper is optional
A summary of the findings
A clear ask with a deadline and a reason
A request for comments on style

questions.hint: A senior reader needs to know what to decide and when.

questions.prompt: In the stronger version, which information helps the reader weigh the recommendation?

options.text: The software that tracks claims and the version used when the review began
The date the review began
The expected effect on time and the annual cost
The names of the reviewers

questions.hint: Costs and benefits allow a decision.

questions.prompt: The summary says the saving is £80,000 but the main text says £800,000. What should you do?

options.text: Use the lower figure to be safe
Remove the figure from the summary
Leave it, as readers will read only the summary and never compare it with the body
Check the source and make the paper consistent before it goes anywhere

questions.hint: Inconsistency between summary and body damages credibility.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the best replacement for 'It is felt that consideration should be given to a number of options'?

options.text: We have set out three options and recommend option 2.
Options have been considered by the team.
It is suggested that the options might be of interest.
A number of options exist for the department.

questions.hint: State how many options there are and which one you recommend.

questions.prompt: Which test best shows that a summary works?

options.text: It uses all the technical terms in the paper
A reader who sees only that page can say what is wrong, what you recommend and what they must decide
It contains no numbers
It is exactly one page long

questions.hint: The summary must stand alone for a busy reader.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the active voice correctly and tells the reader who acts?

options.text: We will remove the second review for low-risk claims from April.
Consideration will be given to the second review.
The second review is to be removed from April for all low-risk claims.
Removal of the second review has been proposed.

questions.hint: Active verbs show who is doing what.

items.title: L9: Judging requests for personal data from other bodies
items.source: Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 2; ICO guidance on disclosing information to the police and other authorities; UK GDPR Articles 5 and 6
items.body:
Departments often receive requests from others to hand over personal data. The answer is never automatic: each request needs a judgement on legal basis, necessity and proportionality, and a record of the decision.

Police and other agencies sometimes ask for data to prevent or detect crime, catch a suspect or collect tax. Schedule 2 of the Data Protection Act 2018 contains an exemption that can allow disclosure where not disclosing would be likely to prejudice those purposes. It is a permission, not an obligation, in most cases, and it does not override the other principles. Ask for a written request that explains who is asking, what data is needed, why, and how not providing it would prejudice the investigation. Disclose only what is necessary. Many forces use a standard form for this. Courts and statutory powers, such as a court order, are different, because they may require disclosure.

A request from a local authority or another department needs a lawful basis for the sharing and a legal power for both bodies, usually in the form of a data sharing agreement or a statutory gateway. A one-off request should still be documented.

A request from a family member or friend does not give them a right to someone's data. Without consent or other lawful basis, the answer is normally no, though you can take their information and pass it on. A supplier who asks for personal data to deliver a contract should have it written into the contract, with the processing limited to instructions.

A journalist's request for personal data is usually handled under FOI, with the personal data exemption considered, or under the journalism exemption in data protection law. Do not give out personal data on the telephone.

Where there is an urgent risk to life, you may share what is necessary to protect vital interests and then record the decision. Always keep a note of who asked, what was decided, why, and what was sent.

questions.prompt: A police officer phones asking for a customer's current address. What is the right response?

options.text: Ask the customer for permission first without telling the police
Ask for a written request that says what is needed, why, and how refusing would prejudice the investigation
Refuse all police requests as a rule
Give the address, since police always have a right to it

questions.hint: The crime exemption can permit disclosure, but it needs a justified, documented request.

questions.prompt: What is the status of the Schedule 2 crime exemption?

options.text: It removes the need to keep a record
It requires disclosure whenever the police ask
It applies only to special category data
It permits disclosure in suitable cases but does not oblige it, and other principles still apply

questions.hint: It is a permission to disclose where non-disclosure would prejudice the purpose.

questions.prompt: A court order requires a department to provide a document containing personal data. How does this differ from a voluntary request?

options.text: It is treated as an FOI request
It is treated as optional
It is ignored if the person objects
The order may legally require disclosure, so the department should comply after checking its scope

questions.hint: A legal requirement is different from a request that the department may choose to meet.

questions.prompt: A customer's sister phones for details of their claim and says she is worried. What should you do?

options.text: Take her information to pass on, but not disclose the customer's data without consent or another basis
Confirm only whether the claim is open
Tell her everything because she is a relative
Ask her to prove she is related

questions.hint: Family connection is not a lawful basis for disclosure.

questions.prompt: A local authority asks for tenants' details to prevent fraud. What is needed before you share?

options.text: A phone call from the local authority's chief executive
A legal power for the sharing, a lawful basis and a record, often with an agreement
Nothing, since both are public bodies
The tenants' bank details

questions.hint: Public bodies still need a legal gateway and a lawful basis.

questions.prompt: A supplier needs customer data to run a contract. Where should the terms for its use be written?

options.text: In the contract, limiting use to the department's instructions
In the supplier's own privacy notice, which sets out how it handles customer data
Nowhere, as suppliers are trusted
In an email from the account manager

questions.hint: Article 28 requires a written contract with a processor.

questions.prompt: A reporter asks for a named official's details. How should the department approach this?

options.text: Release the details to avoid bad press
Refuse to confirm anything about staff
Treat it as an FOI request or press enquiry and consider the personal data exemption
Provide the details by telephone

questions.hint: Personal data is usually protected, so consider the exemption and the public interest.

questions.prompt: A child is at immediate risk of serious harm and a social worker asks for an address. What principle may support disclosure?

options.text: Contract, since the child is a customer
Legitimate interests, since this is not a public task
Consent from the parent, in every case
Vital interests, sharing only what is necessary and recording the decision

questions.hint: Protecting life is a lawful basis in emergencies.

questions.prompt: Why must you keep a note of each disclosure decision?

options.text: To show who asked, what was decided and why, in case the decision is challenged
To satisfy the police
To increase the size of the case file
To avoid the need for a data protection officer

questions.hint: Accountability means being able to explain the decision.

questions.prompt: An organisation asks for 'everything' about a customer, but only needs an address. What principle applies?

options.text: Storage limitation: delete the rest
Purpose limitation: share the data for any new purpose that is helpful
Accuracy: check the whole file
Data minimisation: share only what is necessary

questions.hint: Disclosure should be limited to what the stated purpose requires.

items.title: L9: Publishing statistics safely: small numbers and pre-release
items.source: Code of Practice for Statistics (Office for Statistics Regulation); ONS statistical disclosure control guidance; Statistics and Registration Service Act 2007
items.body:
When a department publishes statistics, it must protect the people behind the numbers and the trust of the public. Two issues are common: disclosure risk from small numbers and the handling of figures before release.

Statistical disclosure control reduces the risk that an individual can be identified. A table that shows 'Ward X, aged over 90, claimants: 1' could identify one person. Methods include suppressing small counts, for example replacing counts under 5 with a symbol, rounding to the nearest 5 or 10, combining categories such as merging age bands, and reducing detail by using a larger area. Suppression needs care: if a total is shown and only one cell is suppressed, the cell can be worked out by subtraction, a problem called secondary disclosure, so another cell must also be protected. A risk assessment should look at the combination of variables, not just one table.

The Code of Practice for Statistics is built around three pillars: trustworthiness, quality and value. Trustworthiness includes independence from political influence, openness about methods and revisions, and equal access: statistics should be released to everyone at the same time. Release times and dates should be announced in advance, and only a small number of people should have pre-release access, which should be as short as possible and published. Pre-release access to figures should be limited to those who need it to prepare a response or to quality assure them.

Revisions and corrections should be handled openly, and a significant error should be corrected promptly with an explanation. Do not use publication to bury bad news by choosing the timing to avoid scrutiny.

Statistics should come with the information users need to interpret them: definitions, sources, quality and limitations. Provisional figures should be labelled as such. Be consistent with earlier releases so that users can compare, and explain any breaks in the series.

questions.prompt: A table of claimants by ward and age shows one ward and age band with a count of 1. What is the concern?

options.text: The person could be identified from the table
The number is below the threshold for a chart
The table is not in sentence case
The ward has too few claimants to be a ward

questions.hint: Small counts risk disclosing information about an individual.

questions.prompt: Which technique is a typical way to reduce disclosure risk?

options.text: Suppressing or rounding small counts
Adding colour to the table
Publishing at a different time
Sorting the table alphabetically by region and by age band

questions.hint: Suppression and rounding make identification harder.

questions.prompt: A table shows a total of 20 and three cells of 8, 9 and a suppressed cell. What is the problem with suppressing only that cell?

options.text: The cells will be sorted automatically so that the missing value shows
The hidden value can be worked out by subtraction
The table will not print
The total will be wrong

questions.hint: Secondary disclosure needs another cell protected too, or a different approach.

questions.prompt: What are the three pillars of the Code of Practice for Statistics?

options.text: Trustworthiness, quality and value
Speed, size and style
Accuracy, access and audit
Honesty, impartiality and integrity

questions.hint: The Code's structure centres on these three areas.

questions.prompt: Why should statistics be released to everyone at the same time?

options.text: Because the law forbids all early use
So that no group has an unfair advantage and trust is maintained
So the press office has less work to do
Because all official statistics are market sensitive and must be released together

questions.hint: Equal access is part of the principle of trustworthiness.

questions.prompt: Who should receive pre-release access to figures?

options.text: The press, to prepare coverage
A small number of people who need it, for as short a time as possible, with the list published
Any minister's adviser who asks
Everyone in the department who is interested

questions.hint: The Code limits pre-release access and requires openness about it.

questions.prompt: Which timing choice would breach the spirit of the Code?

options.text: Publishing on a regular schedule
Labelling provisional figures
Publishing bad news at a time chosen to avoid scrutiny
Announcing release times in advance

questions.hint: Release timing should not be used to manage the story.

questions.prompt: A significant error is found in published statistics. What does the Code expect?

options.text: Leave it unless a user reports the error to the department
Correction at the next annual release
Removal of the whole release
Prompt correction with a clear explanation

questions.hint: Openness about errors protects trust.

questions.prompt: A new method breaks the time series. What should the department do?

options.text: Keep using the old method secretly and publish only the old series
Remove the earlier years
Hide the change in a footnote
Explain the break and its effect so users can interpret trends

questions.hint: Users need to understand changes that affect comparability.

questions.prompt: What should accompany published statistics to help users?

options.text: A list of staff who produced them
A copy of the spreadsheet formulas and the names of the checkers
Definitions, sources, quality information and limitations
The minister's comments

questions.hint: Context allows users to interpret the numbers properly.

items.title: L9: Security judgement: AI tools, aggregation and overseas transfers
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy; Cabinet Office Generative AI Framework for HMG; UK GDPR Chapter V; NCSC guidance on cloud security
items.body:
Modern working raises security questions that have no simple rule, so you need to apply principles. The core approach is to think about the impact of loss or disclosure, to protect information in line with its classification, and to ask the security team when unsure.

Generative AI tools can be useful, but public tools send what you type to an outside company. The Government's Generative AI Framework says that officials should not put sensitive or classified information, or personal data, into public AI tools unless the department has approved the tool and the use. Use only approved systems for OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE material. Check the output, because it may be wrong, and remember that you remain responsible for work you produce with it.

Aggregation, as seen already, can raise the sensitivity of a collection. A spreadsheet listing every employee with home addresses and absence reasons is more sensitive than one record. Treat large extracts with extra care: limit who has them, use approved storage and delete when finished. Combined data can reveal patterns, such as the location of sensitive sites, that individual items do not.

Cloud services are normal in government, but you must use approved services and configure them properly. Personal accounts, such as a private Dropbox, are not appropriate for work files. The NCSC publishes cloud security principles that suppliers must meet.

When personal data is transferred outside the UK, UK GDPR Chapter V applies. Transfers are allowed where there is an adequacy regulation for the destination, or appropriate safeguards such as the International Data Transfer Agreement or standard clauses, or a specific exception. Storing data on a server overseas, or giving a foreign supplier remote access, counts as a transfer. Check with the data protection and security teams before agreeing a supplier, and record the decision. A transfer of OFFICIAL data may also raise security concerns about who can access it, which are separate from data protection.

If you spot a risky practice, speak up and report it. A security culture depends on people asking questions early.

questions.prompt: A colleague wants to paste a draft with customer names into a public AI chatbot to improve the wording. What is the right advice?

options.text: Use a personal account so it is not linked to work
Replace the surname with an initial and continue
Go ahead, as long as the chat is deleted afterwards
Do not, as public tools send input outside the department, unless the tool and use have been approved

questions.hint: Personal data and sensitive content must not go into unapproved public tools.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for work produced with the help of an approved AI tool?

options.text: The AI supplier
The official, who must check the output
The department's IT team
Nobody, since the tool wrote it and the supplier owns the output

questions.hint: AI output can be wrong, and the human remains accountable.

questions.prompt: A spreadsheet extract lists every employee's home address and sickness absence reason. Why does it need more protection than a single record?

options.text: Spreadsheets are classified SECRET
The file is larger than the email limit that applies to attachments
Only absence reasons are personal data
The collection is more sensitive and damaging if lost

questions.hint: Aggregation can raise the impact of a breach.

questions.prompt: A colleague stores work files in a personal cloud account for convenience. What is the main objection?

options.text: It uses too much bandwidth
It is not an approved service and the department loses control of the information
Cloud storage is always less secure than a laptop
It is not allowed to store spreadsheets

questions.hint: Only approved services meet the security and data protection requirements.

questions.prompt: A supplier based overseas needs remote access to a database that contains personal data. How should this be treated?

options.text: As a possible international transfer needing safeguards under UK GDPR Chapter V
As prohibited in every case
As a transfer only if the data is moved physically
As a routine matter needing no checks

questions.hint: Remote access from overseas can be a transfer.

questions.prompt: Which of these can make a transfer of personal data outside the UK lawful?

options.text: A statement that the data is anonymised
The consent of the supplier
An adequacy regulation for the destination or appropriate safeguards such as the IDTA
The destination being in the same time zone

questions.hint: Chapter V provides adequacy, safeguards or exceptions.

questions.prompt: Which is a sensible first step when you are unsure about a new tool or process?

options.text: Use it only outside working hours
Wait for an incident to find out
Try it on a small amount of real data first to see whether anything goes wrong
Ask the security or data protection team before you use it

questions.hint: Early advice avoids incidents.

questions.prompt: Why can combined information reveal more than separate items?

options.text: Patterns and links can emerge that individual items do not show
Combined files are always larger
Combined data is no longer personal
Separate items are always unclassified, however sensitive their contents are

questions.hint: Aggregation can reveal sensitive information by inference.

questions.prompt: You notice colleagues regularly emailing OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE files to personal addresses. What should you do?

options.text: Mention it in a team joke
Copy the practice to keep up
Ignore it because it is so common among colleagues
Report it to the security team or line manager

questions.hint: Reporting risky practice helps to fix it before an incident.

questions.prompt: What does the NCSC publish that is relevant to buying cloud services?

options.text: Cloud security principles that suppliers should meet
A list of approved suppliers
Tax guidance for suppliers
A template for staff contracts and for supplier agreements

questions.hint: The principles help organisations assess supplier security.

items.title: L9: Records management: retention, disposal and FOI offences
items.source: Public Records Act 1958; Freedom of Information Act 2000 section 77; National Archives records management guidance; UK GDPR Article 5
items.body:
Government information is a record, not just data. Good records management means that the right information is created, kept in a way that can be found, held for as long as needed, and then either transferred or destroyed on schedule.

The Public Records Act 1958 requires departments to select records of historical value and transfer them to The National Archives, normally by the time they are 20 years old. Most records are not selected, and are destroyed once they are no longer needed. The retention schedule sets out how long each type of record is kept and what happens at the end. Every department has one. A record's value is judged by operational need, legal requirement, accountability and historical interest.

UK GDPR storage limitation says personal data should not be kept longer than necessary for its purpose. A retention schedule gives the basis for this. Deleting personal data on time reduces risk, and keeping it for ever 'just in case' is a breach of the principle. Equally, destroying a record early can be a problem if it is still needed for a legal or audit reason.

Emails and messages can be records. Decisions made on instant messaging apps should be captured in the formal record. Keep records in the corporate system rather than in personal folders or on personal devices, where colleagues cannot find them.

Section 77 of the Freedom of Information Act makes it a criminal offence to alter, deface, block, erase, destroy or conceal a record with the intention of preventing disclosure when a request has been made. Once a request for information has been received, you must not delete or change the relevant records, even if your routine retention schedule would normally permit destruction. The same principle applies to a subject access request.

When disposing of records, use approved methods and log the destruction. Information asset owners are responsible for the records in their area and decide on their retention within policy.

questions.prompt: By when are public records normally due to be transferred to The National Archives?

options.text: When they are 20 years old
When the minister who created them leaves office
When they are 50 years old
When they are 5 years old

questions.hint: The Public Records Act, as updated, sets a 20-year rule for transfer of selected records.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a retention schedule?

options.text: To list who may read each record
To set how long each type of record is kept and what happens at the end
To record the classification of each document and the names of everyone who may read it
To list the staff who created each record

questions.hint: It guides consistent, lawful retention and disposal.

questions.prompt: Why is keeping personal data forever 'just in case' a problem?

options.text: It is allowed if the data is encrypted
It breaches the storage limitation principle
It breaches the accuracy principle only
It is allowed if the data is classified OFFICIAL

questions.hint: Personal data should be kept only as long as needed for its purpose.

questions.prompt: An FOI request arrives for emails that your retention schedule says may be deleted this week. What should you do?

options.text: Move them to a personal folder
Delete them quietly and tell the requester that the records are not held
Delete them on schedule as policy requires
Keep the relevant records until the request has been dealt with

questions.hint: Destroying records after a request to prevent disclosure is an offence.

questions.prompt: What does section 77 of the Freedom of Information Act make an offence?

options.text: Charging a fee for information
Altering, destroying or concealing a record to prevent disclosure after a request
Refusing a request that is too costly
Replying after the 20 working days

questions.hint: The offence is about interfering with records to stop their release.

questions.prompt: A decision was agreed in a group chat on a messaging app. What should happen to the record of the decision?

options.text: It should be captured in the formal record system
It can stay in the app only
It needs no record if the app is secure
It should be deleted to avoid disclosure, since messages are never records

questions.hint: Important decisions must be recorded in the corporate record.

questions.prompt: Who typically decides how long records in their area are retained, within policy?

options.text: The information asset owner
The most junior member of staff
The press office
The Information Commissioner

questions.hint: Asset owners are responsible for the information in their area.

questions.prompt: Why are personal folders and personal devices poor places to keep work records?

options.text: They cannot be backed up
They are not allowed to hold text documents such as reports or minutes
Colleagues cannot find them and the department cannot control them
They are always slower

questions.hint: Records must be accessible to those who need them.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of destroying a record earlier than its retention period?

options.text: There is no risk if nobody has asked to see the record
There is no risk if the record is classified OFFICIAL
There is no risk, as holding less data is always safer
It may still be needed for a legal, audit or operational reason

questions.hint: Records must be kept for the period required by law and need.

questions.prompt: What should you do after destroying records under the retention schedule?

options.text: Keep a copy of the records in case anyone asks questions later
Log the destruction using an approved method
Tell the requester
Nothing, as it is routine

questions.hint: A log shows records were disposed of lawfully and on schedule.
